Hypnosis, Trauma And The Johari Window Of The Mind

A young man came to me with anxiety and intimacy issues. Medical tests were normal. But emotionally, he felt broken.

Through relaxation-based hypnotherapy, we accessed buried memories of childhood sexual abuse. Consciously, he had “moved on.” Yet the unconscious mind stores emotional imprints long after we think we’ve buried them.

Trauma does not disappear. It changes form. It returns as anxiety, trust issues, emotional numbness, or intimacy blocks.

The Johari Window speaks of 4 parts of self. One is the “unknown area” — hidden from both self and others.

Hypnosis becomes a gentle bridge into this unknown. Not magic. Not mind control. But focused awareness where the mind feels safe to heal.

When hidden pain enters awareness, healing begins.

Therapy isn’t just removing symptoms. It’s reconnecting fragmented parts of ourselves with compassion.

*Counselling as a Path to Emotional Growth*

Many believe counselling is only for crises. In truth, it’s a powerful tool for anyone seeking emotional growth.
Emotional maturity means taking responsibility for your feelings without blaming others, recognizing your patterns, and being open to change. But this is easier said than done. That’s where counselling helps.

In a safe, non-judgmental space, you get to explore your reactions, fears, and beliefs. Over time, you gain clarity, learn healthy coping skills, and grow resilient. You stop reacting from old wounds and start responding from a place of strength.

*Emotional maturity is not perfection — it’s progress. Counselling supports that journey with compassion and insight.*

Being in a marriage where silence replaces conversation breaks you slowly. There are no words to respond to, no fights to resolve—just long, heavy pauses that make you question your worth, your voice, and your place in the relationship. The silent treatment doesn’t shout, but it hurts louder than words.

I reached a point where the loneliness inside the marriage felt heavier than being alone. That’s when I found support through Sanjeev Mittal at Holistic Living Therapy Centre. Therapy helped me understand that this silence was not calm or maturity—it was emotional withdrawal, and it was damaging my mental and emotional well-being.

With gentle yet honest guidance, I began to heal. I learned that asking for communication is not being demanding, and wanting emotional safety is not weakness. Most importantly, I learned that silence used as punishment is a wound that needs acknowledgment, not endurance.

This journey reminded me of a painful truth: love cannot survive where voices are ignored. Healing begins when silence ends—and the right guidance can help you find your voice again.

owner_posts.post_text:
Stress begins to fade when we learn to pause, reflect, and choose peace over pressure. At Samvid, we believe mental wellness starts with awareness and mindful thinking. 🌿

“One thought can change your entire day.”
Take a moment today to choose kindness, calm, and self-awareness. 💙

Why emotionally unavailable relationships keep repeating — and how your patterns shape them.

Most people believe they keep attracting emotionally unavailable partners.
But what I often see in therapy is this, people stay in emotionally unavailable relationships longer than they should.

Not because they don’t know better.
But because something in the pattern feels familiar.

We start:
• Explaining behaviour
• Waiting for clarity
• Overgiving to feel chosen

And slowly, the dynamic gets shaped.
Emotional availability isn’t just about who you meet.

It’s also about what you tolerate, how you respond, and what you choose to stay in.

You've had the conversation. More than once.
And yet you're back at the same place.

It's not that you're not trying. It's that most couples are stuck in a pattern they can't see and no amount of talking fixes what you haven't named yet.

In couples work, I've seen five patterns come up again and again. Each one looks like a communication problem on the surface. Underneath, something else entirely is going on.

Feeling like you’re the only one trying in a relationship is not just painful. It is exhausting.

Usually, it starts with good intentions.
And slowly, the relationship becomes uneven.

Not always because the other person does not care.
But because a pattern gets created where one person over-functions and the other under-functions.

That is why trying harder does not always make things better.
Sometimes, it only keeps the same dynamic going.

Not all relationship issues come from lack of effort.

Sometimes, they come from a difference in how both partners relate to change.

One partner naturally leans toward growth:
They notice patterns
They bring up conversations
They want things to improve

The other leans toward acceptance:
They feel things are fine
They don’t see the same urgency
They prefer things to stay easy

And this creates a repeating tension:
One feels, “We need to work on this”
The other feels, “Why are we creating problems?”

Over time:
• Growth starts feeling like criticism
• Acceptance starts feeling like avoidance

And both partners feel misunderstood.

This is often called the change partner vs acceptance partner dynamic.

It’s not about who is right.
It’s about understanding what each person is trying to protect.

If this resonates, save this—you might need to come back to it.
